pool.prompt: A telecom crew works on a joint-use pole near an energized 7,200V phase-to-ground conductor. What is the MINIMUM rubber insulating glove class required if an authorized employee must work within the minimum approach distance?
choices: Class 00 (rated <=500V AC)
Class 0 (rated <=1,000V AC)
Class 1 (rated <=7,500V AC)
Class 2 (rated <=17,000V AC)
pool.explanation: Class 1 rubber insulating gloves are rated for a maximum-use voltage of 7,500V AC, covering 7,200V phase-to-ground with margin. Class 0 (1,000V) and Class 00 (500V) would be dangerously under-rated. Class 2 (17,000V) would work but is higher than the minimum required.
pool.citation: 29 CFR 1910.137; ASTM D120 glove class voltage ratings.

pool.prompt: An OSP crew splices fiber from a bucket truck in a lane closure on a 45 mph highway during daylight. What is the MINIMUM required hi-vis apparel class?
choices: Class 1 — minimum background material
Class 2 — daytime roadway minimum
Class 3 — required only at night
No hi-vis required — they're elevated, not walking in traffic
pool.explanation: Class 2 hi-vis is the minimum for daytime work in a temporary traffic control zone on a public roadway. Elevation in a bucket doesn't eliminate the struck-by hazard from approaching vehicles. MUTCD and OSHA requirements are based on proximity to a traffic lane.

pool.prompt: Which ANSI Z89.1 hard hat class provides electrical protection tested to 20,000 volts and is required when working near energized distribution conductors?
choices: Class G (General)
Class C (Conductive)
Class E (Electrical)
There is no electrical rating class for hard hats
pool.explanation: ANSI Z89.1 Class E (Electrical) is tested to 20,000V. Class G (General) is rated for 2,200V — insufficient for distribution voltage work. Class C (Conductive) provides no electrical protection at all. Note that the 20kV rating is a lab dielectric test rating, not a safe-contact voltage.

pool.prompt: A crew member is pulling cable through conduit wearing standard leather work gloves. An energized 4,160V conductor is 2 feet away, within the minimum approach distance. Are the leather gloves sufficient?
choices: Yes — leather is a natural insulator and provides some protection
Yes — if the worker is careful not to touch the conductor directly
No — leather work gloves provide zero electrical insulation; rubber insulating gloves (minimum Class 1) are required
Yes — 4,160V is below the threshold where insulating gloves are required
pool.explanation: Leather work gloves provide ZERO electrical insulation — they are rated for mechanical protection only (cuts, abrasion, grip). Being within the minimum approach distance of an energized 4,160V conductor requires rubber insulating gloves rated Class 1 (7,500V) or higher.

pool.prompt: A crew arrives with Class 2 rubber insulating gloves (rated 17,000V) whose last re-test date is stamped 8 months ago. What should they do?
choices: Use them — they're rated for the voltage being worked near
Remove them from service and tag them for laboratory re-testing
Do a visual inspection only; if no cracks are visible, they're acceptable
Use them for today only, then send them for re-testing tomorrow
pool.explanation: Rubber insulating gloves must be re-tested by a qualified laboratory at intervals not exceeding 6 months from the last test date. At 8 months, these gloves are overdue regardless of apparent condition — visual inspection alone cannot detect the micro-cracks or degradation that compromise insulation.
pool.citation: ASTM D120 (6-month in-service retest interval); 29 CFR 1910.137(b)(2)(ii).

pool.prompt: What is the correct voltage-rating order (lowest to highest) of rubber insulating glove classes 00, 0, 1, and 2?
choices: Class 2 (500V) < Class 1 (1,000V) < Class 0 (7,500V) < Class 00 (17,000V)
Class 00 (500V) < Class 0 (1,000V) < Class 1 (7,500V) < Class 2 (17,000V)
All four classes carry the same voltage rating; the number indicates glove thickness only
Class 00 (17,000V) < Class 0 (7,500V) < Class 1 (1,000V) < Class 2 (500V)
pool.explanation: The classes scale upward with the number: Class 00 = 500V AC, Class 0 = 1,000V AC, Class 1 = 7,500V AC, Class 2 = 17,000V AC (with Class 3 and 4 rated even higher, up to 36,000V). Selecting the wrong direction could leave a worker dangerously under-protected.
pool.citation: ASTM D120 glove class voltage ratings.

pool.prompt: What does a worker need to upgrade to if daytime Class 2 hi-vis work runs into low-light conditions (dawn, dusk, overcast)?
choices: No change is needed — Class 2 covers all lighting conditions
Class 3 hi-vis apparel
Downgrade to Class 1 since traffic is lighter at those times
Switch to a hard hat only, no vest required
pool.explanation: Class 3 hi-vis is the higher-visibility standard used for nighttime or low-light conditions and high-speed roadways. Crews should proactively upgrade to Class 3 as lighting degrades rather than waiting to be told.

pool.prompt: Match each PPE item to the class/rating threshold that makes it adequate for the described hazard.

items.label: Rubber insulating glove for a 7,200V phase-to-ground conductor
Hard hat for work near energized distribution conductors
Hi-vis apparel for daytime roadway work
Maximum interval before a rubber glove must be laboratory re-tested

targets.label: ANSI Z89.1 Class E (20,000V dielectric test)

pool.explanation: Each PPE item has a specific minimum rating for its associated hazard: Class 1 gloves for distribution-range voltage, Class E hard hats near energized conductors, Class 2 hi-vis for daytime roadway work, and a 6-month re-test cycle for rubber insulating gloves in service.
